09 The Verifier's Rule, revisited
- **From the first lecture:** [Jason Wei on the asymmetry of verification](https://www.jasonwei.net/blog/asymmetry-of-verification-and-verifiers-law). It is now the guiding rule for the probabilistic half.
- **In one line:** the ease of training AI on a task is proportional to how verifiable the task is. Every task that is possible to solve and easy to verify will be solved by AI.
- **The benchmarks show it.** Graduate STEM exams and competition maths have a correct answer for every question, and decades of past papers. Models ace them.
- **So read benchmarks with care.** Acing a verifiable test with enough examples shows the rule working, not general intelligence.

> If you can verify a task and the data exists or can be collected, a machine can learn it.

[P3] raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md § 06 Label the chunks, then filter
06 Label the chunks, then filter
Mark every chunk with where it sits. That mark is its **label**. The first idea from the chat was lecture numbers. But Verifier's Law comes up in almost every lecture, so a number alone does not say where it is taught. The label needs what each part covers. Our course already has the shape: three modules (images, LLMs, then Module 3), each module has weeks, each week has lectures. Give each module a list of its words.

"Verifier's Law" is on Module 2's list. So send only Module 2's chunks. The rest never reach the LLM.

Is this the keyword fix again? No. There, the LLM had to guess the one word to search the sheet for. Here, it picks one of three modules, and you wrote down what each one covers.

> Sketch: Which lecture teaches Verifier's Law? Three module boxes, each holding chunks. Module 2, LLMs, has a word list with Verifier's Law on it, so its chunks are picked. Module 1, images, and Module 3 stay out.

## Lecture 1: Orientation and State of AI 2026

Held Sat 19 Sep 2026, both tracks, combined theory. [Sheet, code track](../../raw/sheet/code-track.md#sat-19-sep-2026--1-orientation-and-state-of-ai-2026)

Question: why do models improve while businesses earn little from them? Answer: "a verifier gap". [Overview](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-overview.md#orientation-and-state-of-ai-2026)

## What happened, in order

- Week 0: Assignment 1 observation and discovery done, MVP plan still to do. 56 unique industries in the room. [Notes 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#01-where-we-stood-week-0-two-of-three-done)
- A 2023 newspaper project aimed at 10 percent of P&L in time saved and got 2% after eight months. An editor: "this is good, but I still have to spend my time on it". [Notes 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#02-one-sentence-from-an-editor-2023)
- The room's diagnoses (wrong metric, incomplete brief, stakeholders) were true but not the load-bearing failure. [Notes 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#03-the-room-diagnoses-it)
- Four easy answers were killed: a better model, better prompts, more data (the fine-tune did worse), more time. [Notes 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#04-killing-the-four-easy-answers)
- Missing: only the editors knew what a good article looked like, unwritten, so checking cost as much as writing. Hence the Verifier's Law. [Notes 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#05-what-was-actually-missing)
- Two reports: capability climbs, EBIT stays flat. [Notes 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#06-same-failure-at-scale-two-reports)
- Over 5.5 billion dollars in one quarter went to engineers inside enterprises, not models. [Notes 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#07-follow-the-money)
- Verifier example: 15 Ogilvy-inspired criteria scoring copy out of 100, looped until the threshold. [Notes 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#08-what-a-verifier-looks-like-ogilvy-in-15-criteria)
- Round one: an app that adds two numbers gave input, process, output and the golden dataset. [Notes 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#09-the-verify-game-round-one-an-app-that-adds-two-numbers)
- Round two: high school exam, pass mark 33 percent, score 80 percent, output yes. A rule-based verifier. [Notes 10](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#10-round-two-has-someone-cleared-the-high-school-exam)
- Round three: a Rolls-Royce refund, about 7.5 crore. A rule can be gamed, so ask a support executive with ten years of refunds: judgment. [Notes 11](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#11-round-three-a-million-dollar-refund)
- The three boxes: verifiable by a rule (weeks 1 to 4), by judgment (weeks 4 to 8), by nothing yet (the last 4 weeks). [Notes 12](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#12-the-three-boxes-the-next-eight-weeks)

## Numbers to remember

- McKinsey 2026: 1,719 respondents; 80% say AI improved their productivity; 37% report any positive EBIT contribution; 6% high performers. [Notes 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#06-same-failure-at-scale-two-reports)
- Stanford HAI 2026: SWE-bench Verified about 60% to near 100%; 88% of organisations adopted AI; $285.9B US private AI investment in 2025. [Notes 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#06-same-failure-at-scale-two-reports)

- Ode: $1.5B; OpenAI: $4B+, about 150 FDEs; Accenture and Google Cloud: up to 1,000 FDEs. [Notes 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#07-follow-the-money)

## Words it introduced

- Verifier: "A written judgment of how you decide an output is good, usable by a stranger or a model without you." [Notes 14](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#14-what-to-do-next)
- Deterministic system: verifiable by a rule. Probabilistic system: output varies for the same input. [Notes 14](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#14-what-to-do-next)
- Human in the loop: where judgment cannot be articulated, so cannot transfer to a model. [Notes 14](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#14-what-to-do-next)
- Loop engineering: designing the loop of verifier, threshold, improve, re-score, stop. [Notes 14](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#14-what-to-do-next)

## The Verifier's Law

"If you cannot write the verifier, you cannot build the system, and you cannot claim the capability." Lecture 1 named it. [Lecture 1 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#05-what-was-actually-missing)

## How Lecture 1 got there

- A 2023 project for a newspaper's editors saved 2% of time after eight months, against a target of 10 percent of P&L. [Lecture 1 notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#02-one-sentence-from-an-editor-2023)
- Four easy fixes failed: a better model, better prompts, more data, more time. None sat where the failure was. [Lecture 1 notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#04-killing-the-four-easy-answers)
- What was missing: only the editors knew what a good article looked like, and nobody had written it down. [Lecture 1 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#05-what-was-actually-missing)
- So checking the AI draft cost as much as writing it, and writing it yourself was rational. [Lecture 1 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#05-what-was-actually-missing)

## What it is used for

- It explains why domain expertise is valuable in 2026: "the expert is the only source of the verifier". [Lecture 1 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#05-what-was-actually-missing)
- It explains the gap between models and money: "It is not a technology problem. Most experts have never written down how they judge, so every output routes through them." [Lecture 1 notes, 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#07-follow-the-money)
- The question to ask every time: "how do I verify whether this output is correct? No answer, no build." [Lecture 1 notes, 12](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#12-the-three-boxes-the-next-eight-weeks)

## Common mistake

- Asking the LLM to write your verifier. "It returns the average of every expert, and the same slop anyone gets." [Lecture 1 notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-01-notes.md#08-what-a-verifier-looks-like-ogilvy-in-15-criteria)

## Lecture 10: Tool calling and MCP

Lecture 10, Tool calling and MCP, was held on Sat 31 Oct 2026 for both tracks, as combined theory. [Sheet, code track](../../raw/sheet/code-track.md#sat-31-oct-2026--10-tool-calling-and-mcp)

It kept asking GPT-OSS 120B one question, "Which track should I choose in 100x Engineers cohort?", to find why the answer was made up and how to supply the missing context automatically. [Notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#01-the-test-query)

## What happened, in order

- The bare model invented tracks: 1 out of 10, a hallucination. [Notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#01-the-test-query)
- A short block on the real tracks scored 5; the full C8 curriculum as CSV text scored 7, still naming Zapier. [Notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#02-more-context-helps-but-doesnt-cure-it)
- Andrej Karpathy's framing: the model has no hallucination problem; the LLM assistant does. [Notes, 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#03-why-models-hallucinate)
- In OpenOrca training data, fewer than 5% of records were the model saying it doesn't know. [Notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#04-trained-never-to-say-no)
- A better prompt or temperature at 0 did not remove it. [Notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#05-two-fixes-that-dont-work-alone)
- A golden pair found the cause: the curriculum never names a UI builder; adding Lovable, Google AI Studio, Antigravity closes the gap. [Notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#06-diagnose-with-a-golden-pair)
- Automating the paste needs a data source and a bridge; almost nobody finished the live challenge. [Notes, 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#07-automating-the-paste-a-data-source-and-a-bridge)
- An API alone can't be the bridge: the file can't send requests, the model is probabilistic. [Notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#09-why-an-api-alone-cant-be-the-bridge)
- JSON was elected as the common language; only the server is kept as the bridge. [Notes, 11](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#11-the-server-is-the-bridge)
- Function calling, shipped by OpenAI on 13 June 2023: the model asks the server to act for it. [Notes, 12](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#12-function-calling-the-reverse-call)
- Q&A: let the server search a keyword list per source instead of routing in English; this is indexing. [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)

## Numbers to remember

- Scores for the same question: 1 (no context), 5 (real tracks), 7 (full curriculum CSV). [Notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#02-more-context-helps-but-doesnt-cure-it)
- The real tracks: two career tracks (Entrepreneurship, Career Accelerator) and two execution paths (Code, No Code). [Notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#01-the-test-query)
- OpenOrca: about 2.9 million records; of roughly 30,000 scrolled, fewer than 5% declined. [Notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#04-trained-never-to-say-no)

## Words it introduced

- Golden pair: the ideal input and the ideal output, written before the run; one golden dataset entry. [Notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#06-diagnose-with-a-golden-pair)
- Hallucination: "A confident answer that lands in factually wrong territory." [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)
- LLM assistant: "The whole system around the model: client, APIs, data, tools." [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)
- Context: "The data that reaches the model inside its context window." [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)
- Temperature: "Controls randomness in the output." [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)
- Data source: "The trusted store that must hold the context before any bridge can help." [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)
- Function calling (tool calling): the model asks a deterministic server to run a request for it. [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)
- Tool call: "The model's JSON naming the function and its arguments." [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)
- Execution environment: your backend, which runs the tool call and returns the result. [Notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#13-from-the-qa)

## After the lecture

- One step is added to Practice set 1: pick one Automate or Augment task and write its golden pair first. [Notes, 14](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#14-practice)
- Run it bare, then with context, in the GroqCloud playground; score both out of 10 and note what was missing. [Notes, 14](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#14-practice)
- Then Practice set 2, write the eval: about 45 minutes, in a new tab of the sheet. [Notes, 14](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#14-practice)

## Lecture 6: Databases and domain modelling

Lecture 6, "Databases and domain modelling", was on Sat 10 Oct 2026 for both tracks, as combined theory. [No-code sheet](../../raw/sheet/no-code-track.md#sat-10-oct-2026--6-databases-and-domain-modelling), [code sheet](../../raw/sheet/code-track.md#sat-10-oct-2026--6-databases-and-domain-modelling)

Its question: Aarav's app can think but cannot remember, so what is worth storing? [Overview](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-overview.md)

## What happened, in order

- So far: UI to your server to the LLM on Groq's machine; each call needs "address, action, key, package". [Notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#01-the-whiteboard-so-far)
- Outsource your thinking, not your understanding: a retired Llama 3 model in Groq's docs gives a 404. [Notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#02-outsource-your-thinking-not-your-understanding)
- The LLM sits outside your server because of its size. [Notes, 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#03-where-should-each-piece-live)
- Aarav's app forgets: on Tuesday the call returns a 200, but the model has no idea which plan he means. Every request starts from nothing. [Notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#04-aaravs-app-forgets)
- Memory dies when the app stops. Storage sits outside the app, on disk. [Whiteboard](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-whiteboard.md#memory-dies-storage-survives)
- The fix, without saying "database": keep a `memory.txt`. After every reply, write down who said what, with the date and time. On the next request, send the file along with the prompt. [Notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#05-derive-it-before-you-name-it)
- So `memory.txt` stores one shape: who, what, when. [Notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#09-three-questions-give-the-shape)
- Start with the file and move up only when it breaks. [Notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#05-derive-it-before-you-name-it)
- Storage and the key live on your server, because on the user's machine the user can wipe it and anyone can read it. [Notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#06-where-does-storage-live)
- The high-level design of Aarav's app, with storage (7) as a file on your server. [Notes, 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#07-the-high-level-design)
- Worth storing is "the least you need to carry on next time": write the questions your app must answer tomorrow. [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#08-what-is-worth-storing)
- Things become tables, facts become columns, links get a shape. [Notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#09-three-questions-give-the-shape)
- Number rows with an `id` (the key); a link is a column on the many side; many-to-many needs a third table. [Notes, 10](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#10-keys-and-pointers)
- Two rules: "History is a row, not a cell." "Rows for facts, files for bytes." [Notes, 11](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#11-two-rules-that-save-you-later)
- Aarav's model: eight tables. [Notes, 12](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#12-aaravs-model)

## Numbers to remember

- GPT-OSS-120B needs about 65 GB of memory, plus GPUs; a 421-million-parameter model about 2.5 GB. [Notes, 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#03-where-should-each-piece-live)
- gpt-oss-120b: 117 billion parameters in 15 files; a laptop has 16 GB. [Whiteboard](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-whiteboard.md#some-work-does-not-fit-in-that-box)
- A key sent to the browser let a stranger spend the $10 of credit. [Notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#06-where-does-storage-live)

04 The CRUD Quiz: Create, Read, Update, Delete
The game's actions were four words. They are the four things you can do to anything stored: **Create, Read, Update, Delete**, or CRUD. On the wire, each is spelled as an HTTP method.

| Aarav's action | CRUD | Method and address |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opens the page listing his past diagnoses | Read | GET /diagnoses |
| Submits his Friday workflow for the first time | Create | POST /workflows |
| Fixes one field: "weekly" becomes "every Friday" | Update | PATCH /workflows/7 |
| His UI resends the whole workflow with the fix | Update | PUT /workflows/7 |
| Removes an old workflow | Delete | DELETE /workflows/7 |

PUT and PATCH are both Update. PUT replaces the whole thing; PATCH changes part of it.

> Sketch: The rule: if the cost of issues Y exceeds the car's cost X, refund. A coral question underneath: who supplies Y, and was it engineered a day before the warranty ended? On the right, a support executive with ten years of refunds, accountable if wrong, asked whether the story smells right. The output is binary: yes or no.

- **The case.** Should a Rolls-Royce customer get a refund? About 7.5 crore in India, close to a million dollars. The output is yes or no.

- **Judgment-based verification.** Before the final output, ask a support executive who has done refunds for ten years and answers for mistakes. Same input, different output depending on whether the story smells right.
- **Judgment has two sources:** a human, or an artificial one. Some transfers from human to model once written down, as Ogilvy's did. Some does not.

The list of numbers that places a text is its **embedding**. The program that makes it is an **embedding model**. Ranking passages by how close their embeddings sit to the question's is search by meaning.

Which embedding model do you use?

[P3] raw/course/04-what-is-learning/one-job-repeated.md § Next token, again and again
Next token, again and again
A language model does one job: score every possible next token, pick one, add it to the end, and go again.

> Caption: Finish both sentences, one token at a time.

> Principle 8Everything a model writes is the next token, guessed from patterns held in its dials.

## Lecture 11: Tool calling and MCP

Lecture 11, "Tool calling and MCP", was on Fri 13 Nov 2026 for both tracks, a combined practical (Tool Bench, Groq). [Sheet, Lecture 11](../../raw/sheet/code-track.md#fri-13-nov-2026--11-tool-calling-and-mcp)

It asked how an LLM can use one shop's Google Sheet: the model asks for an action, a deterministic server executes it, the verifier proves what happened. [Lecture 11 overview](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-overview.md#tool-calling-and-mcp-part-2)

## What happened, in order

- 01: Four layers; the lecture was Protocol and Tooling. [Lecture 11 notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#01-where-tools-and-mcp-sit)
- 02: The question reused from Lecture 10, "Which execution track should I choose in 100x?": the LLM fills gaps. [Lecture 11 notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#02-from-lecture-10-the-llm-fills-gaps)
- 03: Priya's shop: pasting the sheet is repetitive, error-prone, stale and doesn't scale. [Lecture 11 notes, 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#03-priyas-shop-the-paste-problem)
- 04: The rule: revenue counts every order except cancelled ones. Golden pair: the kettle, 4,980. [Lecture 11 notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#04-the-sheet-and-its-one-rule)
- 05: Only the question, the instruction and the data reach the LLM. [Lecture 11 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#05-what-reaches-the-llm)
- 06: The server is the bridge. [Lecture 11 notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#06-the-server-is-the-bridge)
- 07: Function calling: send, decide, request, execute, return, answer. [Lecture 11 notes, 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#07-function-calling-the-llm-asks)
- 08: The tool schema has five parts: name, description, parameters, required, types. [Lecture 11 notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#08-the-tool-schema)
- 09: 400, 401, 404, 500 and an empty result each need a different message. [Lecture 11 notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#09-when-the-tool-fails)
- 10: Verify the execution record, not the sentence. [Lecture 11 notes, 10](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#10-verify-the-record-not-the-sentence)
- 11: MCP, one standard for every tool. [Lecture 11 notes, 11](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#11-mcp-one-standard-for-every-tool)
- 12: Host, client, server, end to end. [Lecture 11 notes, 12](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#12-host-client-server)
- 13: Five steps for Lecture 12. [Lecture 11 notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#13-tomorrow-lecture-12)

- The Lecture 10 question scored 1 out of 10 with no context, 5 with a short description, 7 with the full curriculum; it still named Zapier. [Lecture 11 notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#02-from-lecture-10-the-llm-fills-gaps)

- Order 1046, a kettle, is cancelled and left out of revenue. [Lecture 11 notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#04-the-sheet-and-its-one-rule)
- Revenue: Kettle 4,980, Mug set 3,960, Linen 3,870, Oak board 1,890. [Lecture 11 notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#04-the-sheet-and-its-one-rule)
- Tool card tests passed out of 5: empty card 3; "Gets a lecture by number" 4 or 5; the full card 5, every run. [Bench notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-bench-notes.md#04-write-the-tool-card-against-tests)

- The whole bench costs about 35 calls. [Bench notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-bench-notes.md#01-the-bench)

- Source of truth: where the real records live. Deterministic bridge: the server between the LLM and the data. Also host, client, server and A2A. [Lecture 11 notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#13-tomorrow-lecture-12)
- Context window: everything the LLM can see while answering. Tool schema: name, description, parameters, required fields, types. [Lecture 11 notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#13-tomorrow-lecture-12)
- Execution record: the tool, the arguments, the result and whether it succeeded. Verifier: the expected record, written before the run. [Lecture 11 notes, 13](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#13-tomorrow-lecture-12)

Now ask: "Which lecture teaches Verifier's Law?" A fair question. But the tool takes only a lecture number, 1 to 19, and this question has none. So no tool call happens. What does the LLM answer: an error, the right lecture, or a wrong one?

Done means it answers the questions
> Sketch: Three product questions and the pointer path that answers each. Aarav's last conversation, every message in order: users to conversations to messages. Every plan this workflow ever got: workflows to diagnoses, oldest first. Which screenshot went with which message: messages to attachments. Then try to break it: a message with no conversation is refused.

A model is not done when it looks tidy. It is done when it answers what the product must ask. Write your own three questions first, trace each answer along the pointers, then try to create a wrong state and make sure the model refuses it.

23 · Your turn

[P3] raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md § 09 Three Questions Give the Shape
09 Three Questions Give the Shape
`memory.txt` stored one shape: who, what, when. Aarav's app needs more: his conversations, his workflows, and every plan each workflow got. The lab splits "what is worth storing?" into three questions:

1. What are the things? Can the app create, read, update and delete one on its own, and can there be many? A conversation passes. "9:12 am" fails: it only says when one message was sent, so it is a fact. Each thing gets a **table**. In the lab it is a block on Aarav's board first, and becomes a table in Level 6.
2. What does each thing have? The facts you need to recreate one. For a message: who said it, what, and when. Each fact is a **column**. Tone is a fact on a plan today. If users could save named tones, it would become a thing. What the product does with it decides.
3. How do they connect? Ask two questions, both ways. Can one conversation have many messages? Yes. Can one message sit in many conversations? No. The two answers give the link its **shape**: one-to-many (most links), many-to-many (both yes: a third table), or one-to-one (both no, and rare: often the two are one table).

This is **domain modelling**: the smallest description of your user's world that still answers the product's questions.

Practise it: [Level 1](https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-06-databases-and-domain-modelling/playgrounds/modelling-lab#s1) for things, [Level 2](https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-06-databases-and-domain-modelling/playgrounds/modelling-lab#s2) for facts, [Level 3](https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-06-databases-and-domain-modelling/playgrounds/modelling-lab#s3) for links.

## 03 Count the shared words

How do you know which passage answers "Which lecture teaches Verifier's Law?" Most of the chat said: search for the keywords. Then the next question: "verifier" is in many passages, so which one wins? One answer from the chat: the one where the words come up most.

Start simpler and test it. Give each passage a score: how many different words it shares with the question. Send the top 3.

```
def score_shared(question, passage):
    q = set(words(question))           # the words in the question
    p = set(words(passage["text"]))    # the words in the passage
    return len(q & p)                  # how many words are in both
```

It found 5 of the 10: A, E, F, G and I. It missed B ("Why is the model making things up?") and J ("What does CRUD stand for?"). Shared words work when people type the words your notes use. Most people do not.

The ten questions with known answers are your **golden set**: ten golden pairs, the idea from [Lecture 10](https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-10-tool-calling-and-mcp/notes#s06). Count how often the right passage lands in the top 3, over the whole set: that is **recall at 3**. Here it is 5 of 10, or 50%. The 3 is how many passages you keep, called **top-k**. You pick k to fit your budget.

> Know the right answers first. Then count how often your search finds them.

Asked at Google and at Meta: "How do you know your retrieval works?" The strong answers in the chat named the number. "I keep a small set of questions where I know which passage holds the answer. After every change I count how often that passage lands in the top 3. Counting shared words found 5 of 10. That is where I started."

- A search box has "no memory, no context"; chat won because it holds context. [Lecture 3 notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-03-notes.md#09-the-vote-that-lost)

## Lecture 6: it forgets, so keep a file

- Tuesday: Aarav types "I implemented the plan, but hit a problem." A 200 comes back; the model has no idea which plan. [Lecture 6 notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#04-aaravs-app-forgets)
- "Memory dies. Storage survives." Storage sits outside the app, on disk. [Lecture 6 whiteboard](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-whiteboard.md#memory-dies-storage-survives)
- The fix, without saying "database": keep a `memory.txt`; after every reply write who said what, with the date and time; send the file with the next prompt. [Lecture 6 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#05-derive-it-before-you-name-it)
- "Start with the file and move up only when it breaks." [Lecture 6 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#05-derive-it-before-you-name-it)
- The file and the key live on your server: on the user's machine the user can wipe it and anyone can read it. [Lecture 6 notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#06-where-does-storage-live)
- "`memory.txt` stored one shape: who, what, when." [Lecture 6 notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-notes.md#09-three-questions-give-the-shape)
- Eight tables and their pointers, kept outside the app: "That is a **database**." [Lecture 6 whiteboard](../../raw/lectures/lecture-06-whiteboard.md#storage-with-a-shape-has-a-name)

## Lecture 7: the file dies

- After step 04 the server "forgets every plan the moment it answers." [Lecture 7 notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-07-notes.md#09-step-04--gradio-becomes-a-client-tonight)
- "The file dies." Plans saved to `memory.txt` work locally and fail on Vercel. [Lecture 7 notes, 11](../../raw/lectures/lecture-07-notes.md#11-next-lecture-8-saturday-6-pm)

## Lecture 8: tables in Supabase

- Step 05, `memory.txt` in four lines: read the file, run `diagnose`, build a line with time, workflow and plan, write it all back. Most people missed the timestamp. [Lecture 8 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#05-step-05--memorytxt-in-four-steps)
- Where a file breaks: 60,000 lines for 100 users, two writers at once (a race condition), a small machine returning 500 to everyone. [Lecture 8 notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#06-where-a-file-breaks-and-where-it-does-not)
- Deployed, step 05 fails anyway: "Vercel's file system is read-only, so the write fails with a 500." [Lecture 8 whiteboard](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-whiteboard.md#a-file-is-enough-until-people-write-at-once)
- PostgreSQL, rented from Supabase, reached with the same four dials: address, action, key, package. [Lecture 8 notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#08-the-same-four-dials)
- Modelling Lab to database: thing to table, fact to column, link to foreign key, id to primary key. [Lecture 8 notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#09-from-the-whiteboard-to-tables)
- "Four file lines became one insert." `diagnose` and the route did not change. [Lecture 8 notes, 10](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#10-steps-07-and-08--the-server-remembers)

## Lectures 10 to 14: getting the right data to the model

- Lecture 10: **context** is "the data that reaches the model inside its context window"; automating the paste needs a data source and a bridge. [Lecture 10 notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#04-trained-never-to-say-no), [Lecture 10 notes, 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md#07-automating-the-paste-a-data-source-and-a-bridge)
- Lecture 11: pasting a sheet is repetitive, error-prone, stale and does not scale; a server fetches from the trusted source when a question needs it. [Lecture 11 notes, 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#03-priyas-shop-the-paste-problem)
- Lecture 11: "If it doesn't reach the LLM, the LLM can't use it." [Lecture 11 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md#05-what-reaches-the-llm)
- Lecture 12: a tool, `get_lectures(track)`, reads the curriculum sheet when the model asks. [Lecture 12 notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#01-step-1-the-function)
- Lecture 13: retrieve, augment, generate. "Swap the sheet for Supabase and step 1 is still retrieval." [Lecture 13 notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#01-name-the-three-steps)
- Lecture 13: with tables from your Lecture 6 domain model, the LLM writes SQL and the server runs it on Supabase. [Lecture 13 notes, 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#07-to-label-it-know-the-domain)
- Lecture 14: search 183 passages, send the best 3. Their embeddings fit a plain file; Supabase's pgvector waits for a real limit. [Lecture 14 notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-14-notes.md#01-the-pile-and-the-ten-questions), [Lecture 14 notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-14-notes.md#08-do-you-need-a-vector-database)

- Where a file breaks: two writers at once lose a plan (a race condition), and a small machine runs out of memory and returns 500 to everyone. [notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#06-where-a-file-breaks-and-where-it-does-not)
- Deployed, step 05 fails anyway: Vercel's file system is read-only, so the write fails with a 500. [whiteboard, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-whiteboard.md#a-file-is-enough-until-people-write-at-once)
- Storage moved to PostgreSQL rented from Supabase, called with the same four dials: address, action, key, package. [notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#08-the-same-four-dials)
- The Modelling Lab became tables: thing to table, fact to column, link to foreign key, id to primary key, via `schema.sql`. [notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#09-from-the-whiteboard-to-tables)
- Four file lines became one insert; `diagnose` and the FastAPI route did not change. [notes, 10](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#10-steps-07-and-08--the-server-remembers)
- Gradio was replaced by a text box, a button and one fetch. [whiteboard, 16](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-whiteboard.md#rip-off-gradio-a-text-box-a-button-one-fetch)
- Without RLS, one `select *` returns Aarav's workflows to anyone with the URL and a key. [notes, 11](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#11-whose-row-is-this)

## Numbers to remember

- 100 users, 10 workflows a day, 60 days: 60,000 lines. [notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#06-where-a-file-breaks-and-where-it-does-not)
- A file is fine for one user, under about ten operations a day, a fixed window. [notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#06-where-a-file-breaks-and-where-it-does-not)
- The logged request: 2.77 seconds, status 200. [notes, 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#03-read-the-logs-on-someone-elses-machine)
- The bet: 6 of 10 early-career people map one repeated workflow and build an app. [notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#04-what-is-worth-storing)
- Supabase is free up to 50,000 monthly active users and 500 MB. [notes, 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-08-notes.md#07-postgres-rented-from-supabase)

Passages found by search in the 100xEngineers Cohort 8 course pages:

[P1] raw/lectures/lecture-09-notes.md § 04 The query that broke it
04 The query that broke it
> Which track should I choose in 100x Engineers cohort?

- **The shape was right.** A decision framework, assessment questions, a mapping from answers to tracks, a checklist. Close to what a good mentor would give.
- **The data was wrong.** Front-end, back-end, full-stack, data and ML, DevOps, product, security. None of them exist.
- **The real choice has two axes.** A career track (entrepreneurship or career acceleration, set by your North Star) and an execution path (code or no-code, set by your background).
- **We fixed the constraint:** one answer, no follow-up questions. Under that, an assessment framework is the right template.
- **Right template, wrong data: hallucination.** It is why this model, as is, cannot be the career coach on the 100x website.

> Sketch: Input: which track should I choose in 100x Engineers cohort? The output is a long page: a self-assessment framework, ticked, and a list of tracks. The tracks it recommended, all struck through: front-end, back-end, full-stack, data and ML, DevOps, product, security. Missing data caused the hallucination. The real choice has two axes: career track, entrepreneurship or career acceleration, and execution path, code or no-code.
>
> Caption: Right template, wrong data.

[P2] raw/lectures/lecture-10-notes.md § 01 The test query
01 The test query
> Which track should I choose in 100x Engineers cohort?

> Sketch: The question goes into the bare GPT-OSS 120B model. Out comes a list of tracks that do not exist, crossed out, scored 1 out of 10. Below, the missing data: two career tracks and two execution paths.
>
> Caption: The bare model had never seen the real tracks.

- **The setup.** GPT-OSS 120B in the GroqCloud playground: a bare model, not a chat product, because that is what you build on.
- **The truth is small.** Two career tracks (Entrepreneurship, Career Accelerator) and two execution paths (Code, No Code). The site changed after the model's training cutoff.
- **Score: 1 out of 10.** A confident, well-formatted answer built on facts the model doesn't have is a **hallucination**. The diagnosis from [Lecture 9](https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-09-llms-from-first-principles/notes#s04): the data was missing.

[P3] raw/lectures/lecture-11-notes.md § 02 From Lecture 10: the LLM fills gaps
02 From Lecture 10: the LLM fills gaps
"Which execution track should I choose in 100x?" With no context the LLM scored 1 out of 10, with a short description 5, with the full curriculum 7. It still named Zapier, which is nowhere in the file. [Lecture 10 has the runs.](https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-10-tool-calling-and-mcp/notes#s02)

- **It predicts the next token.** It does not look anything up.
- **It fills a gap with the likely answer,** and does not tell you it did.
- **Confidence is not proof.**
- **A better prompt and a lower temperature help, and neither adds a fact.** At temperature 0 you get the same wrong answer every time.

To find what went wrong, write a [golden pair](https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-10-tool-calling-and-mcp/notes#s06): the ideal input and the ideal output, decided before you run the LLM. Then compare.

> Reducing randomness does not create missing knowledge.

You have tools to look things up. The 100x brain: what 100xEngineers Cohort 8 has been taught, as pages a person approved. Read the index first, open the pages you need, and answer only from pages you opened, naming the page. For dates and titles the schedule page wins. If the pages do not hold the answer, say "not known". This brain knows the course, not the person asking.

Question: The question "Which execution track should I choose in 100x?" came back in more than one lecture. Which lectures, and what did each one do with it?

Answer in a few short sentences.

The question: asked which track to choose, the model on its own makes up the answer. Today you write the tool in Python. [Lecture 12 notes](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#one-tool-call-then-an-mcp-server)

## What happened, in order

- 01: A plain Python function, `get_lectures(track)`, reads one track's tab of the curriculum sheet and returns each lecture with its tools. [Lecture 12 notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#01-step-1-the-function)
- 02: The model can't see your function. It reads a card: a name, what it does, and what to pass in. The Groq request gets one new field, `tools`. [Lecture 12 notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#02-step-1-the-card)
- 03: The model replies with a tool call, not an answer. Your code runs the function and sends the result back until the model stops asking. It asked twice, once per track, and never touched the sheet. [Lecture 12 notes, 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#03-step-1-the-tool-call)
- 04: `mcp_server.py` puts the same function at an address any app can reach. `@mcp.tool` writes the card from the name, the docstring and the type hint. `fastmcp list` returns the card; `fastmcp call` runs the tool. [Lecture 12 notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#04-step-2-the-mcp-server)
- 05: The thing the model was missing in Practice set 1, step 04, is your first tool. [Lecture 12 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#05-your-turn)

- Model: `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Groq. [Lecture 12 notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#02-step-1-the-card)
- A 429 error means wait a minute and run again. [Lecture 12 notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#02-step-1-the-card)
- The server runs at http://localhost:8000/mcp. [Lecture 12 notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#04-step-2-the-mcp-server)

## Words it introduced

- Tool: a function your code runs when the model asks for it. [Lecture 12 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#05-your-turn)
- Card: the description of a tool that the model reads: its name, what it does, and what to pass in. [Lecture 12 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#05-your-turn)
- Tool call: the model's reply naming a tool and what to pass in. A request, not an action. [Lecture 12 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#05-your-turn)
- MCP server: tools at an address, so any app can list them and call them. [Lecture 12 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#05-your-turn)
- FastMCP: the Python library that turns a function into an MCP server. [Lecture 12 notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-12-notes.md#05-your-turn)

## Lecture 13: Retrieval-augmented generation

Lecture 13, "Retrieval-augmented generation", Fri 20 Nov 2026, "combined theory", Arc 3: Context. [Code sheet](../../raw/sheet/code-track.md#fri-20-nov-2026--13-retrieval-augmented-generation)

- Both tracks; the no-code sheet has the same row. [No-code sheet](../../raw/sheet/no-code-track.md#fri-20-nov-2026--13-retrieval-augmented-generation)
- The sheet's Status still says "Planned". [Code sheet](../../raw/sheet/code-track.md#fri-20-nov-2026--13-retrieval-augmented-generation)
- It was taught: the notes are dated "20 November 2026 · Both tracks". [Notes](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md)
- The question: how do you send the LLM only the few chunks that matter? [Overview](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-overview.md)

## What happened, in order

- 01: "When is Lecture 12?" The room named the three steps: retrieval, augmentation, generation. Together, RAG. [Notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#01-name-the-three-steps)
- 01: MCP solves a scaling problem: 100 tools and 10 LLMs means 1,000 connections. [Notes, 01](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#01-name-the-three-steps)
- 02: "Which lecture teaches Verifier's Law?" has no number, so no tool call; the LLM made up "Lecture 12: Security and cryptography." [Notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#02-break-it-a-question-with-no-number)
- 03: Three fixes: check for a number, LLM picks the keyword, paste the whole sheet. Only pasting can work; it still said Lecture 12, since the sheet has only dates and titles. [Notes, 03](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#03-three-fixes-from-the-chat)
- 04: Pasting everything crossed the context window and the API answered 400. A bigger LLM only moves the line. [Notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#04-paste-it-all-until-it-does-not-fit)
- 05: Chunking works, but every question pays for every chunk. [Notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#05-cut-it-into-chunks)
- 06: Label chunks by module, then filter: "Verifier's Law" is on Module 2's list. The labels make an index. [Notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#06-label-the-chunks-then-filter)
- 07: Labelling needs domain knowledge. With structured data, the LLM writes SQL from the schema; the server runs it on Supabase. [Notes, 07](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#07-to-label-it-know-the-domain)
- 08: A plain tool call is RAG in principle; most teams hit the budget first. [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)
- 09: Do all seven stations of the Retrieval Bench. [Notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#09-now-do-the-retrieval-bench)

## Numbers to remember

- The tool takes a lecture number, 1 to 19. [Notes, 02](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#02-break-it-a-question-with-no-number)
- The lectures sheet is 2,834 tokens. [Notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#04-paste-it-all-until-it-does-not-fit)
- GPT-OSS 120B on Groq reads about 128,000 tokens; a chat guess was 1 million. [Notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#04-paste-it-all-until-it-does-not-fit)
- Five or six pastes crossed the line. The largest LLMs read 1 to 2 million tokens. [Notes, 04](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#04-paste-it-all-until-it-does-not-fit)
- A million tokens in chunks of 100,000 is 10 chunks, 10 calls; 1,000 chunks, 1,000 calls. [Notes, 05](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#05-cut-it-into-chunks)
- Amazon phones: 60,000, then 2,000, 23 Samsung, 7 in budget. [Notes, 06](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#06-label-the-chunks-then-filter)
- One Retrieval Bench question used 424 tokens. [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)
- A bill can grow from $100 to a million dollars; the same questions can cost $100 or $10,000. [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)

## Words it introduced

- RAG: "Fetch the data that matters, add it to the prompt, let the LLM write." [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)
- Context window: "The most tokens an LLM reads at once." [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)
- Chunk: "A piece of the data small enough to fit." [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)
- Label: "A tag that says where a chunk sits (module, week, lecture), so you can filter." [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)
- Index: "The labels read like a contents page: go straight to the right chunk." [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)
- Domain knowledge: "Knowing the things in your data well enough to label them." [Notes, 08](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#08-tool-call-or-rag)

## After the lecture

- Run the Retrieval Bench with a Groq key (from the Tool Bench, or console.groq.com/keys). [Notes, 09](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md#09-now-do-the-retrieval-bench)
- No practice set or due date is written. [Overview](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-overview.md)

## Pages

- Overview, the lecture in one line plus the bench: https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-13-retrieval-augmented-generation/ [Overview](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-overview.md)
- Notes, with sketches and "Check yourself": https://100x-curriculum.vercel.app/c8/module-2/lecture-13-retrieval-augmented-generation/notes [Notes](../../raw/lectures/lecture-13-notes.md)

See also: [Retrieval-augmented generation](../concepts/retrieval-augmented-generation.md), [Chunk](../concepts/chunk.md), [Label](../concepts/label.md), [Index](../concepts/index.md), [Domain knowledge](../concepts/domain-knowledge.md)

[P1] raw/practice/what-to-build-idea-to-app-notes.md § 02 A North Star has four elements
02 A North Star has four elements
> Sketch: A North Star drawn as a bridge. On the left a person, labelled role or identity: AI real estate consultant. On the right a box, $15,000 a month, labelled level, income or scale. Above, a calendar card: December 2026, the timeline. The bridge between them is the specific thing: automating lead gen, the element most people left out.
>
> Caption: Four elements. The specific thing is the bridge from who you are to the number.

Two North Stars were pulled apart on the whiteboard. Kaushik: by December 2026, a dental tourism company running fully on AI agents except the patient calls, at $500 a month recurring. A C6 student: by December 2026, an AI real estate consultant in the UAE automating lead generation for agencies, at $15,000 a month.

- **Timeline.** A date, six months out. A North Star for this cohort, not for your life.
- **Role and identity.** What people will call you. "Leading an AI-powered engineering workflow" is a task, and begs the question of who leads it.
- **Level, income or scale.** The quantity you will have on the date. Money, a designation, an appraisal or a measured impact, as long as it is a number.
- **The specific thing.** The one workflow that bridges the role to the number. For the UAE consultant, automating lead gen. Almost everyone left this out.

Three from chat, reviewed live:

[P2] raw/practice/what-to-build-idea-to-app-notes.md § 02 A North Star has four elements (2)

- **Saiteja.** Passed all four: growth marketer or indie maker, marketing the AEO tool he already built, to 1K MRR.

> The North Star defines the goal. It never explains the route.
